clinicalPearls: The primary (hereditary) form of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, presenting with the triad of digital clubbing, periostosis of the long bones and pachydermia (thickened, furrowed facial and scalp skin)
Caused by defects in prostaglandin E2 metabolism, through recessive variants in HPGD (the degrading enzyme) or SLCO2A1 (the prostaglandin transporter), leading to raised prostaglandin E2 levels
Typically begins around adolescence, is more common and more severe in males, and progresses over years before stabilising
Skin changes include coarse thickened facial skin, deep scalp folds (cutis verticis gyrata) and oily skin with excessive sweating
Periostitis causes limb pain and swelling, and joint effusions may occur
The key clinical task is to distinguish primary disease from secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, which signals underlying lung malignancy, cardiac or other visceral disease
Management is symptomatic, addressing pain and, where troublesome, the skin and joint manifestations, with reassurance once secondary causes are excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Pachydermoperiostosis is caused by impaired inactivation of prostaglandin E2 due to biallelic variants in HPGD, encoding the enzyme that degrades prostaglandin E2, or in SLCO2A1, encoding the transporter that delivers prostaglandin E2 for degradation. Either defect raises circulating and tissue prostaglandin E2, which promotes periosteal new bone formation, soft-tissue and dermal proliferation and vascular changes. Clinically this manifests as digital clubbing, periostosis of the tubular bones with limb pain, and pachydermia with thickened, furrowed skin and increased sweating. The same pathway is implicated in secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, but in the primary form the prostaglandin excess is intrinsic rather than driven by an underlying visceral disease.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from lung malignancy or chronic pulmonary disease
Rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathies
Cutis verticis gyrata from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating symmetrical periosteal new bone along the long bones
Chest imaging to exclude an underlying pulmonary or mediastinal cause of secondary disease
Bone scintigraphy where the extent of periostosis needs characterising
Thyroid function and growth hormone/IGF-1 testing to exclude acropachy and acromegaly
HPGD and SLCO2A1 molecular genetic testing to confirm primary disease
Assessment of urinary or plasma prostaglandin E2 metabolites where available
redFlags: Rapid onset of clubbing and periostosis in an adult, strongly suggesting secondary disease and an occult malignancy
Respiratory symptoms, haemoptysis or weight loss pointing to underlying lung pathology
New cardiac or hepatic signs suggesting a visceral cause of secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
Disproportionate or asymmetrical bone pain warranting exclusion of another process
reference.prognosis: The primary disease is benign and self-limiting, typically progressing over years before stabilising, with morbidity from bone and joint pain and cosmetic skin changes rather than reduced life expectancy; recognising and excluding secondary causes is what matters most for outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming primary pachydermoperiostosis without excluding secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and its sinister causes
Missing an underlying lung malignancy in an adult presenting with new clubbing and periostosis
Mistaking the coarse facies for acromegaly without appropriate endocrine testing
Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance and family implications
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Relieve periostosis-related bone and joint pain with NSAIDs, using a COX-2 selective inhibitor such as etoricoxib that also targets the underlying prostaglandin E2 excess
Consider colchicine for inflammatory skin features and flares, and a bisphosphonate for refractory periostitis pain
Manage pachydermia and cutis verticis gyrata with topical retinoids, botulinum toxin, or cosmetic and plastic surgery for disfiguring scalp folds
Provide symptomatic care for excessive sweating and oily skin
Exclude secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from lung malignancy, cardiac or other visceral disease with chest imaging before attributing features to the primary disorder
Confirm the diagnosis with HPGD and SLCO2A1 genetic testing and offer genetic counselling for this recessive condition
Coordinate rheumatology, dermatology and metabolic bone input
